outcome: Nothing since 26 January 2024 settles, restricts or moves the Poisson distributional claim about prime divisors of Mersenne numbers that the bullet names; the one in-window paper that engages the conjecture (Kovač and Luca, arXiv:2506.04883, June 2025) uses Gillies' heuristic as an input for a different quantity, the number of divisors τ(2^p−1), and proves results about f(2n)/f(n) rather than about the conjecture. No AI system is credited with anything bearing on this problem, and the Wikipedia article still describes the conjecture as open.
problem_asks: The bullet asks one thing: for Mersenne numbers M_p = 2^p − 1 with p prime, the prime divisors of M_p have a particular distribution. Parts: (a) for an interval [A, B] (the Wikipedia article takes A < B < √M_p; Ehrman's and Wagstaff's wording takes the limit as B/A and M_p grow), the number of prime divisors of M_p lying in [A, B] is Poisson distributed. (b) The Poisson mean is the expression the article gives: log(log B / log A) when A ≥ 2p, and log(log B / log 2p) when A < 2p. The bullet itself states only (a); (b) is the article's and Ehrman's specification of the same claim, so I list it as part of the conjecture as written. Not asked by the bullet, but drawn by Gillies as consequences in the article: the number of Mersenne primes below x is about (2/log 2)·log log x; the expected number of Mersenne primes M_p with x ≤ p ≤ 2x is 2; the probability that M_p is prime is about 2·log(2p)/(p·log 2). These are consequences, not parts of the bullet, and the later pass should decide whether they count.

events.what_happened: Donald B. Gillies stated the conjecture in 'Three new Mersenne primes and a statistical theory', Mathematics of Computation 18 (1964) 93–97 (DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-1964-0159774-6), in the same paper that announced three new Mersenne primes. He supported it with a heuristic argument and empirical data (Wikipedia; Wagstaff 1983 as described in search excerpts). I could not open the 1964 paper itself (the AMS page and the DTIC technical-report copy both returned HTTP 403). The statement recorded here comes from the Wikipedia article and from the descriptions of Ehrman and Wagstaff. The conjecture refines earlier suggestions of I. J. Good (1955) and Daniel Shanks (1962) according to the article. Date given as 1964 (the journal year). A 2017 slide deck by Attila Pethő attributes the conjecture to 'D.B. Gillies, 1963'; I treat that as a citation slip, not a separate event.
events.delivers: Conjecture only; establishes nothing. States the Poisson claim for prime divisors of M_p in [A, B] with the two-case mean, plus the consequences listed in the article. Gillies' support is heuristic and empirical.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: no part is established by this event.
events.directly_checkable: The conjecture is a claim about all primes p in a limit. Checking it by hand means computing prime divisors of specific M_p in specific intervals; Ehrman (1966) and Wagstaff (1983) did this for finite ranges (see those events).
events.doubts: Lenstra objected (reported in the Wikipedia article and in Wagstaff 1983 as described in search excerpts) that the conjecture cannot take B as large as M_p, because similar reasoning contradicts the prime number theorem. The article records this as an objection, not a refutation. I could not locate Lenstra's objection in a primary source. A search excerpt attributes to Everest, Rogers and Ward a remark that the heuristic is unlikely to become a proof; I did not open that survey.
events.direction: Asserts a probabilistic distributional claim for all primes p in a limit. It is a conjecture, not a result, so it does not cut for or against the claim by itself.

events.what_happened: J. R. Ehrman, 'Prime Divisors of Mersenne Numbers', technical note TN 66-40, dated September 1966 in the INSPIRE record description (the header was not readable in my fetch), later published as 'The number of prime divisors of certain Mersenne numbers', Mathematics of Computation 21 (1967) 700–704 (DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-1967-0223320-1; the bibliography of Wagstaff 1983 and an arXiv reference list give these details). The note describes two tests of Gillies' conjecture: a test of the mean number of divisors and a test of their Poisson distribution. The OCR shows primes 100,000 < p < 300,000 grouped into 80 bins of width 2,500, with divisors q < 2^31 computed (the OCR reads '231'). The OCR does not show the test outcomes; the results tables are unreadable to me. A search excerpt describes a chi-squared comparison reported as 'satisfactory'; I did not verify this. Wagstaff (1983) says Ehrman 'sharpened Gillies' conjecture slightly and supplied more empirical evidence'. Date given as 1966, the earliest public version I found.
events.revisions: TN 66-40 (1966) and Math. Comp. 21 (1967) 700–704 are the same work in two versions; I could not confirm they are identical.
events.delivers: Numerical evidence for the Gillies distributional claim over a finite range of exponents (primes roughly 10^5 to 3×10^5, divisors below 2^31). A finite-range check of a claim about all primes; it establishes nothing about the claim in general.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, including the claim for all p and all intervals in the limit.
events.directly_checkable: The tests are computations on divisor counts of M_p for listed primes; reproducible from factor tables. I did not reproduce them.
events.doubts: The reported test outcomes were not readable to me, so I cannot say what the tests showed beyond the search-excerpt description. The ranges tested are finite and the tests are limited in power against a claim about the limit as B/A and M_p grow.
events.direction: Supports the conjecture numerically on a finite range, as far as I could read; no result against it is reported in the text I could read.

events.what_happened: Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr., 'Divisors of Mersenne numbers', Mathematics of Computation 40 (1983) 385–397 (DOI 10.1090/S0025-5718-1983-0679454-X). Per its abstract as quoted in search excerpts and per the article's reference list, it adds to the heuristic and empirical evidence for a conjecture of Gillies, lists large prime divisors of Mersenne numbers for 17000 < p < 10^5, derives the Mersenne-prime consequences from the conjecture with A = 2p and B = M_x/2, and discusses Lenstra's objection. The AMS page returned HTTP 403 and the Scribd copy was unreadable, so I read these points from secondary descriptions and not from the paper. Wagstaff's 1983 paper is also the source the article cites for the Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff predictions.
events.delivers: Heuristic and empirical support for the Gillies distributional claim over a finite range of exponents, and derivations of the stated consequences from it. Not a proof. Search excerpts disagree about who wrote that a proof of the heuristic is unlikely; the attribution to Everest, Rogers and Ward is unresolved.
events.remains: All of problem_asks: the paper supports the conjecture and does not establish it.
events.directly_checkable: Lists prime divisors of Mersenne numbers that can be checked by direct division for the stated exponents; I did not check them.
events.doubts: Lenstra's objection is discussed here according to search excerpts: Wagstaff reportedly addresses Lenstra's claim that B cannot be taken as large as M_p (Wikipedia: because similar reasoning contradicts the prime number theorem). I could not read either argument. The predictions of the rival Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff heuristic differ from Gillies' by a constant of about 11% according to the article; both remain conjectures.
events.direction: Supporting evidence, consistent with the Gillies claim on the range treated; not a result against it as far as I could read.

events.what_happened: Vjekoslav Kovač and Florian Luca, 'On the number of divisors of Mersenne numbers', arXiv:2506.04883 (math.NT), first submitted 5 June 2025. Opened abstract (arXiv abs page) and the HTML of v4. Main result as the abstract states it: with f(n) = sum over 1 ≤ k ≤ n of τ(2^k − 1), the ratios f(2n)/f(n) are unbounded, motivated by Erdős's question (erdosproblems.com problem 893), with conditional results on divergence to infinity and numerical tests. Gillies' conjecture enters only as an input. Section 1.2 invokes 'classical Gillies' approximation [12]' for the number of prime divisors of 2^n − 1 greater than A. Section 4.2 says 'Gillies [12] used this reasoning to approximate the number of divisors of the numbers 2^p−1 for prime p' and 'even conjectured that this number behaves like a Poisson-distributed random variable with mean λ', and that his model was 'statistically tested, criticized and refined by subsequent authors [7, 21]' (Ehrman 1967 and Wagstaff 1983 per the reference list). The authors describe their model as partially heuristic. erdosproblems.com credits Kovač and Luca 'building on a heuristic independently found by Cambie (personal communication)'.
events.revisions: v2 10 Jun 2025; v3 8 Dec 2025 (per search excerpt: text reorganised, experimental section expanded, results unchanged); v4 3 Feb 2026 (arXiv comment: 'incorporated editorial suggestions').
events.delivers: For Gillies' conjecture: nothing established. The paper applies the Gillies heuristic to estimate τ(2^n − 1) for large n and compares an approximation with actual values (search excerpt: for 1001 ≤ n ≤ 1100; not verified in the v4 text I read). Its theorems concern f(2n)/f(n), a sum of divisor counts, not the Poisson distribution of prime divisors in intervals. The conditional results rest on further conjectures; a search excerpt names one bounding the number of distinct prime divisors of the cyclotomic values Φ_d(2), and another about Mersenne indices with record divisor counts. I did not read those statements in the v4 text.
events.remains: All of problem_asks. The paper neither proves nor refutes the distributional claim or the mean formula, and it does not test the Poisson distribution of prime divisors in [A, B].
events.time_since_posted: about 16 months since v1 (to 11 Oct 2026); no public engagement with its use of the Gillies model found. A third-party review site (The Moonlight) carries summaries of the paper that a search excerpt describes as AI-written; I did not open that page, and it is not a reading of the mathematics.
events.directly_checkable: The τ(2^n − 1) comparisons and the divisor-count tests are computations on Mersenne factorisations, reproducible with factor tables; the paper's text names Wolfram Mathematica and the Alpertron factoring calculator for its numerical work. I did not reproduce them.
events.doubts: Scope question, not a doubt about the paper's theorems: the Gillies model in the other sources concerns the number of prime divisors of M_p in [A, B] (Ehrman; the Wikipedia article), while Section 4.2 applies it to 'the number of divisors' τ(2^p − 1). The text I read does not say whether the authors take the Gillies count to be the prime-divisor count, the full divisor count, or both. The later pass should check Section 4.2 directly before treating this paper as touching the conjecture. The main unconditional result is about a different quantity, and the conditional parts depend on other conjectures.
events.direction: Does not cut for or against the Gillies distributional claim. It uses the claim as a heuristic input and reports that the model's refinements matter little when A is large (search excerpt, not verified in the v4 text).

events.what_happened: Samuel S. Wagstaff Jr., 'Two Mersenne Prime Conjectures', Journal of Integer Sequences 28 (2025), Article 25.7.2. The abstract, opened on the journal page: 'We discuss two conjectures about Mersenne numbers, an old one and a new one. Heuristic arguments support both conjectures.' The page does not mention Gillies. A search excerpt identifies the old conjecture as the New Mersenne conjecture of Bateman, Selfridge and Wagstaff; the new conjecture's content was not visible to me. I did not open the PDF. A separate Purdue PDF (homes.cerias.purdue.edu/~ssw/chen.pdf, outline headings 'The 1989 New Mersenne Conjecture' and 'Chen's Mersenne Conjecture of 2025') returned only metadata, and it does not mention Gillies in what I could read.
events.revisions: Received 1 Sep 2025; revised version received 27 Sep 2025; published 4 Dec 2025 (journal page). The first public posting, if any, was not found, so no first-argument date is recorded.
events.delivers: Heuristic support for two conjectures about Mersenne numbers, as far as the abstract shows. Nothing about the prime divisors of 2^p − 1 or about Gillies' distributional claim is visible in the abstract.
events.remains: All of problem_asks, as far as I could establish.
events.direction: Not stated on the abstract page. Supports two conjectures heuristically; no bearing on the Gillies claim is visible.

events.what_happened: Jesús Domínguez, arXiv:2603.08994 (math.NT), first submitted 9 March 2026; a later version is dated 14 March 2026 (search excerpts). It appears in search results under two titles, 'Divisor Structure of p−1 in Mersenne Prime Exponents' and 'Arithmetic Bias in the Distribution of Mersenne Prime Exponents and the Divisor Structure of p−1'. The arXiv abstract page was not opened; the description comes from search excerpts. Per those excerpts: it defines S(p) = log τ(p−1)/log log p and reports that Mersenne prime exponents show elevated S(p) within local exponent windows relative to nearby primes; the effect is described as moderate, and the author says no analytic mechanism is established. It cites the Wagstaff heuristic for the probability that M_p is prime as background.
events.revisions: v1 9 Mar 2026; a later version 14 Mar 2026 (search excerpts, which word one point differently).
events.delivers: Nothing about the prime divisors of 2^p − 1. It studies τ(p−1) over Mersenne prime exponents, a different quantity from the number of prime divisors of M_p in an interval.
events.direction: Not about the direction of the Gillies claim. Discounted: different quantity (exponent p−1) and different question.

events.what_happened: Zebediah Engberg and Paul Pollack, 'The reciprocal sum of divisors of Mersenne numbers', arXiv:2006.02373, first submitted 3 June 2020, version 2 on 13 August 2020 (opened abstract page). Studies the reciprocal sums of divisors, and of prime divisors, of 2^n − 1 (sums of 1/p), determines their maxima over n ≤ x asymptotically conditional on the Elliott–Halberstam conjecture and the Generalised Riemann Hypothesis, and addresses a conjecture of Pomerance and a question of Murty, Rosen and Silverman. The abstract page does not mention Gillies or the Poisson model.
events.revisions: v2 13 Aug 2020 ('Made several clarifications and corrections. Added new section on generalizations').
events.delivers: Conditional asymptotics for the maximum of reciprocal prime-divisor sums of 2^n − 1. A different quantity from the number of prime divisors of M_p lying in an interval; no bearing on the Poisson claim.
events.direction: Not applicable: a neighbouring result on a different quantity, discounted under the scope test.

disputes.summary: Gillies' Poisson model and the Lenstra–Pomerance–Wagstaff heuristic predict constants about 11% apart for the count of Mersenne primes and related quantities (Wikipedia article). Both are conjectures; the article says the Gillies model 'disagrees with the widely accepted (but also open)' LPW conjecture. Not a priority dispute; recorded so the later pass sees the rival prediction.

Year of the conjecture: 1964 in the Mathematics of Computation citation (Wikipedia) and in most sources; 1963 in Pethő's 2017 slides ('D.B. Gillies, 1963'). One search excerpt also reports Ehrman's 1966 note as dated 1963 in one place. Recorded as a citation discrepancy; the 1964 paper was not readable to me to settle it.

summary: Gillies' conjecture (Gillies, Math. Comp. 1964) says that for M_p = 2^p − 1 the number of prime divisors of M_p in an interval [A, B] is Poisson distributed, with mean log(log B/log A) if A ≥ 2p and log(log B/log 2p) if A < 2p; the bullet asks for the distributional claim, and the article's mean formula is part of that claim. Sources read: the Wikipedia article (revision 1364886556, last edited 19 July 2026 per the fetch; it still says the conjecture 'remains open' and carries a January 2014 tag asking for an expert mathematics check), the Wikipedia list of unsolved problems (the bullet appears in its prime-number material, with the link to the article), the Wikipedia 'Mersenne conjectures' article, the Ehrman 1966 note via INSPIRE (OCR partial, results unreadable), the Kovač–Luca arXiv abstract and HTML v4, the Wagstaff 2025 journal abstract, the Engberg–Pollack and Ford–Luca–Shparlinski arXiv abstracts, the erdosproblems.com entry 893, and Pethő's 2017 slides. The original 1964 paper and Wagstaff's 1983 paper could not be opened (HTTP 403 at AMS and DTIC; unreadable Scribd copy), so their contents are taken from descriptions, and I have flagged that wherever it matters. Within the window (since 26 January 2024), the only item that engages the conjecture is Kovač and Luca (5 June 2025). They use the Gillies model as a heuristic: Section 1.2 calls it a 'classical Gillies' approximation' for prime divisors of 2^n − 1 greater than A, and Section 4.2 applies it to 'the number of divisors' τ(2^p − 1), citing Ehrman and Wagstaff as having tested and refined it. Their theorems concern f(2n)/f(n), where f sums τ(2^k − 1); they answer Erdős problem 893 in the negative (no finite limit), a result erdosproblems.com credits partly to a heuristic found independently by Stijn Cambie. Whether the authors' τ count is the prime-divisor count of the conjecture is a reading question I could not settle from the text I read. Their result therefore moves the quantity they name, not the quantity the bullet names, and I record it as an event rather than a discount because the conjecture appears in it. The other in-window items are Wagstaff's 2025 'Two Mersenne Prime Conjectures' (its abstract does not mention Gillies; the old conjecture is the New Mersenne conjecture) and Domínguez's March 2026 preprint on τ(p−1) over Mersenne exponents (search excerpts only). Neither bears on the Gillies claim. Earlier support comes from Ehrman (1966 note, 1967 journal; finite-range tests, results unreadable to me) and Wagstaff (1983; heuristic and empirical support, and a discussion of Lenstra's objection that B cannot be taken as large as M_p). No source I read records a proof, a refutation, a counterexample, a Lean formalisation, or a bound moving on the conjecture's own quantity. Lenstra's objection is reported second-hand; I could not find his text. The conjecture is open per the article. No AI system is named anywhere in the sources I read in connection with this problem: the Kovač–Luca text names Wolfram Mathematica and the Alpertron factoring calculator for its numerical work (not AI), and the fetched text has no AI statement. Third-party AI-generated review summaries of that paper exist (The Moonlight, per search excerpts) but are not the authors' account and I did not open them. The broader 2026 AI-and-mathematics news that surfaced (Erdős problems solved by GPT-5.x-class models, AlphaEvolve, an OpenAI claim about a unit-distance conjecture, July 2026 blog claims) concerns other problems; none names Gillies' conjecture or Mersenne prime divisors in the excerpts I saw.
competing_reading: Kovač and Luca could be read as an in-window event that moves the problem's status. Their numerical and conditional results are built on Gillies' Poisson model, and if 'the number of divisors' in Section 4.2 is taken to mean the Gillies prime-divisor count in intervals, the paper amounts to a numerical test of the conjecture that moved nothing it names. The opposite reading is that nothing_found should be true: no in-window item tests or proves the distributional claim, and the Kovač–Luca use is a heuristic input for τ(2^p−1), a different quantity. I recorded the paper as an event (not a discount) because it is in-window and engages the conjecture, and left the scope call to the later pass.
what_would_settle_it: (1) The full text of Kovač and Luca, Section 4.2 and the sentence that introduces 'the number of divisors', to settle whether the Gillies count they use is the prime-divisor count or τ(2^p−1), and whether any numerical comparison in the paper tests the interval-distribution claim itself. (2) The 1964 Gillies paper and the 1983 Wagstaff paper in full (AMS and DTIC were unavailable to me), for the exact statement and the treatment of Lenstra's objection. (3) Lenstra's objection in a primary source; I could not find one. (4) Any 2024–2026 paper that proves, refutes or tests the Poisson claim for prime divisors of 2^p−1 over unbounded ranges; the arXiv search for 'Gillies' returned 81 hits, none on the conjecture, and the search engine found none, but a title-and-abstract search for 'Poisson' with 'Mersenne' on arXiv returned zero results, so this remains a search-coverage limit rather than a settled absence.

The statements of the conditional conjectures (cyclotomic prime divisors at 2; Mersenne indices with record divisor counts) and the Section 4.2 numerical comparison for 1001 ≤ n ≤ 1100 were seen only in search excerpts and are not verified. judgement.why: Nothing in the record proves, refutes, restricts or bounds the Poisson claim about prime divisors of M_p in intervals. Gillies 1964 only states the conjecture (none). Ehrman and Wagstaff 1983 test it numerically over finite exponent ranges (instances, journal-published hence digested). Kovač–Luca use the Gillies heuristic as an input for theorems about f(2n)/f(n), a different quantity; it bears on the problem without settling anything, so none rather than variant. Wagstaff 2025 discusses other Mersenne conjectures with no visible link to Gillies (none); its undated first posting is still placeable after the snapshot because the journal received it in September 2025. Domínguez (τ(p−1)) and Engberg–Pollack (reciprocal divisor sums) are different questions (variant). No AI system is credited anywhere.
judgement.doubts: Kovač–Luca's Section 4.2 applies Gillies' model to τ(2^p−1); whether any numerical comparison there tests the interval-distribution claim itself was not settled, but even if it did, it would be a finite-range check (instances). The Wagstaff 2025 PDF was not opened, so a Gillies-related heuristic inside it can't be ruled out entirely.
